questions.q: Picture a company with a sales database, website logs, product photos and PDF contracts. How would a data lake treat all of that?
options: Convert everything into tidy tables before saving
Keep it all in one place, as is, side by side
Keep only the sales database and drop the rest
Keep one separate store for each kind of file
questions.explain: That is the whole idea. AWS, IBM, Google Cloud and Microsoft all describe a lake as one central store that keeps data in its original form, structured or not.

questions.q: Which sentence best captures the big difference between a lake and a warehouse?
options: A warehouse is always bigger than a lake
A lake can only hold images and PDFs
A lake sets the structure when you read the data, a warehouse checks it before saving
A lake is a database for reports, a warehouse is for backups
questions.explain: It comes down to timing. Microsoft says a lake uses schema-on-read and a warehouse uses schema-on-write. Same data, but the tidying-up happens at a different moment.

questions.q: A team dumps files into a lake for two years with no catalog, no rules and no owner. What are they most likely to end up with?
options: A faster lake, because nothing slows it down
A smaller lake, because old files delete themselves
A data swamp, where good data is hard to find or trust
A warehouse, because lakes turn into one over time
questions.explain: IBM warns that without a management layer a lake can decay into a swamp. Standards, a catalog and clear access rules from day one are the cure.

questions.q: In AWS's Athena example, the same question costs $15 on a plain text file and $1.25 on compressed Parquet (checked Oct 2026). What is the lesson?
options: Files are allowed to sit as is, but the format you pick changes the bill
Parquet files are always free to query
Text files cannot be stored in a lake
Cloud prices change every time you ask a question
questions.explain: Athena bills by how much data it scans. Compression and a column-friendly format like Parquet mean it reads far less. Keep in mind it is AWS's own illustration, not a benchmark.

questions.q: Someone says, "We bought a data lake." What does the post say is closer to the truth?
options: A lake is a single product you install
A lake is a set of parts: storage plus ingestion, a catalog, permissions and query tools
A lake is another name for a warehouse
A lake only exists once you have a lakehouse
questions.explain: No single product is the data lake. It is a set of parts you choose, and storage like S3 is only the first one.
